source: That branch of the lake of Como which extends southwards between two unbroken chains of mountains, and is all bays and gulfs as the mountains advance and recede, narrows down at one point into the form of a river, between a promontory on one side and a wide shore on the other; and the bridge which here links the two banks seems to emphasize this transformation, and to mark the point at which the lake ends and the Adda begins, only to become a lake once more where the banks draw farther apart again, letting the water broaden out and expand into new gulfs and bays. The country bordering the lake, formed by the deposits of three great torrents, is backed by two neighbouring mountains, one called San Martino, and the other, in the Lombard dialect, the Resegone, from its saw-like row of peaks; so that on first seeing it — so long as it is in profile — looking northwards, for instance, from the ramparts of Milan — one can pick it out at once, on the name alone, from the vast and lengthy range of other mountains of obscurer name and more ordinary form. For a considerable stretch the country rises slowly and continuously; then it breaks up into little hills and valleys and into steep and level tracts, following the structure of the two mountains and the erosion of the water. The shore itself, intersected by the beds of torrents, is almost entirely gravel and pebbles; the rest is fields and vineyards, and scattered towns, villages and farms, with here and there a wood extending right on up the mountain-side. Lecco, which is the largest of these towns and gives its name to the district, lies on the lakeside not far from the bridge, and is even apt to find itself partly in the lake when this is high; it is a big town nowadays, well on the way to becoming a city. At the time of the events which we are about to describe, this township which was already of some importance, was also fortified, and so had the honour of housing a commandant and the advantage of a permanent garrison of Spanish soldiers, who taught modesty to the wives and daughters of the town, tickled up the shoulders of an occasional husband and father, and, towards the end of summer, never failed to scatter themselves among the vineyards, to thin out the grapes and lighten the labours of the vintage for the peasants. Paths and tracks used to run — and still do — from one to another of these villages, from the mountain heights to the lakeside, and from one precipice to the other. Sometimes they run steep, sometimes level, and often drop suddenly and bury themselves between two walls, from which, when one looks up, only a patch of sky and some mountain peak can be discerned. Sometimes they come out on open terraces; thence the eye ranges over prospects of varying extent, always full of interest and always changing, as each point of vantage takes in different aspects of the vast landscape, and as one part or the other is foreshortened, or stands out, or disappears. One can see a piece here, another there, and then again a long stretch of that great varied mirror of the water; on this side the lake is shut in at one end, or rather lost among the ins and outs and groupings of the mountains, then spreads out again between more mountains, unfolding one by one, and reflected upside down in the water with the villages on the shores; on the other side is more river, then lake, then river again, losing itself in a shining coil among the mountains, which follow it, getting smaller and smaller until they too are almost lost in the horizon. The very spot from which so many different views can be seen itself appears in views from every side. The mountain on whose foothills you are walking unfolds its cliffs and pinnacles above and around you, each standing out on its own and changing at every step, turning what had just seemed a single ridge into a whole series of ridges, and showing on a height something that a moment before had seemed down on the shore; the quiet and cosy character of these foothills pleasantly tempers the wildness around, and is a foil for the grandeur of the rest of the landscape.

rows.text:
The channel that narrows between the African shelf and the low limestone table of Lampedusa, which lies aslant the traffic of two continents like a stone dropped short of its throw, runs shallow where the current slackens and deepens again where the shelf breaks off, and it carries southward, in a long tilted band that the charts render in four gradations of blue, a body of water whose surface, dimpling and flattening by turns, seems at every hour to be gathering itself in order to arrive somewhere, to press against the island's western flank until the flank gives back a fringe of white, and then, having spent that pressure, to slide off toward the harbour mouth and lose its name.

The island itself, which rises nowhere above a hundred and thirty metres, which wears no forest and hardly any soil, which the wind has been at long enough to plane the rock, keeps its whole northern coast a cliff and its southern one a scoop of pale sand; the cliff drops sheer where the strata part, the sand shelves out so gradually that a hull may ground a hundred paces from the dry, and between them the land holds the temperature of an oven long after the sun has gone.

Along the eastern shoulder the limestone is quarried into terraces that no one now tends, and the low walls run down to the water and stop, as though the dividing of the ground had at some point ceased to mean anything.

Below the terraces lies the Cala Ponente, which the fishermen once used for the drying of nets; two coastguard cutters ride there at moorings now, and a third, whose hull carries the grey of the Guardia di Finanza, lies further out.

From the promontory above the Cala one sees the whole eastern approach, where the sea lifts in long swells and the swells fall in, and one can watch a vessel for forty minutes before it enters the roads; the light off the water is a hard light, which the radar mast on the ridge appears to cut into segments.

The mast, which was raised to extend the surveillance of the strait, which stands on a concrete pad among the caper bushes, turns without sound through its arc, and beneath it the pale road runs to the Contrada Imbriacola, where the reception centre stands behind a double fence, where the buses arrive at first light and the roll is read aloud twice, so that each person may be assisted into the register and then, once the register is complete and the photographs are taken, be conducted onward.

Between the fence and the shore lies the boat graveyard, its timbers stacked to a height of four metres, and the salt has taken the paint from every hull.

Nothing is hidden here: the ground offers no cover, the light gives nothing back, the rock is bare and the scrub is knee-high, and the whole coast can be read from the ridge as one reads a table, provided the haze lifts.

At the harbour the water lies quiet and glassy: the cutters swing to their chains, and the sea inside the mole shows the mast doubled and inverted, the mast shown upright on the ridge and shown standing on its head in the water, the reflection swaying as the wake crosses it.

Beyond the mole the water opens again to a great pale plain, uninterrupted to the horizon; a line runs across it which nothing in the water marks, which no swell or discolouration betrays, and which exists only in the logbook and on the plotter screen, so that a hull crossing it in the dark, without altering course or speed, ceases to be a vessel at sea and becomes an arrival, the water beneath it ceasing to be open sea and becoming, by the same stroke of the pen, territorial.

In these years the shoreline is being altered by the works, which advance a few metres each season.

Whoever comes to the island in August, when the ferries are full and the terraces of the Via Roma are loud, will find the harbour a place of ordinary business, and if he walks out past the last houses, past the fuel tanks and the tuna sheds, toward the low ground where the rock goes yellow, he will come upon a cemetery of hulls that no signboard names, and he will understand what the island is for.

The channel that runs south from the last Sicilian headlands, narrowing where the shelf drops away beneath it, is bounded on either hand by the long swells and the flat calms that give the water its two faces, and it carries, in the season of the sirocco, a traffic which the charts do not mark, so that anyone standing on the cliff at first light and looking outward may see the surface stretch and darken as the wind crosses it, and may see, where a low grey hull idles at the horizon with its engines cut, that the vessel is waiting to be met, since the men aboard have been instructed to render assistance until the coordinates are logged and the record is closed.

The island itself, which lies nearer to the African plate than to the peninsula that administers it, whose limestone is white to the point of glare, whose harbour bends inward like a cupped palm to hold what the current delivers, is a low table of rock set in an immensity of blue: the wind scours it, the salt cures it, the summer bleaches every surface it can reach.

Along the eastern shore the cliffs break down into a series of coves where the water clarifies to nothing over the pale floor; and there, where the depth is four metres and reads as one, the boats come in.

The Cala that the pilots know by its bearing, a notch of shingle beneath a scree of stone, receives them: it is the one landing that a hull without a keel can survive, whose approach requires no light.

The sea in that reach seems to open, widening from the mouth of the cove until the eye loses its far edge, and then to close again, tightening between the shoals as the swell compresses in the narrows; and the same water, which will presently spread once more into the great dilated plain beyond the headland, appears from the cliff to breathe.

The white patrol cutter that stands off the point at dusk, its wake unspooling behind it, whose hull number is legible at two miles through glass, is doubled in the glassy lee below the cliff, where the reflection hangs inverted, its bow pointing landward while the vessel itself points out, so that the observer has two cutters to account for whenever the surface flattens and the light holds.

The men on deck do not appear to hurry, and their movements read at that distance as a kind of housekeeping, a tidying of the water's edge.

At a certain line, invisible in itself, the water ceases to be one thing and becomes another; the line is drawn nowhere on the surface, but a transponder marks it, and a duty officer enters the crossing in a ledger before the hull has changed its heading by a degree.

Twelve miles out the sea is called high, and beyond that it is called free, and inside it is called territorial, though nothing in the colour changes, nothing in the depth changes, nothing in the wind or the set of the current declares the boundary to anyone aboard.

Northward the shelf tilts down and the blue thickens, and off the shoal that the fishermen call the Table, where the bottom rises to within a fathom, the water pales to milk again; and it is here, in these very years, that the traffic is shifting month by month, its routes lengthening westward as the agreements multiply, so that the crossing takes longer now to reach the same shingle than it did before the funding was renewed.

There is no lighthouse on that side, only a mast whose lamp turns all night without illuminating anything.

Everything one sees from the cliff at dawn — the calms and the swells, the cutter, the ledger, the shingle — belongs to a single continuous motion which the coastline merely interrupts, and if the surface seems at that hour to lie still and the island seems to float, it is only because the eye, which cannot register a movement so slow, has not yet learned to read it; and the sea, which will unfold all of this in its own time, goes on gathering and releasing: gathering, releasing, gathering again.

The channel that lies between the two capes, and that narrows where the shelf lifts under it, comes down out of the open water in a long southward reach, dilating and closing again according to the run of the banks below, until it gathers itself between a marl headland on the one hand and a low apron of rubble on the other, and becomes a road, a corridor, a measured thing with a name in three languages, whose current, felt as a drag on the tiller, and setting always a little east of the heading a helmsman would choose, continues to widen as it goes, so that the boats that come up from the south cannot say, when the last loom of coast has gone, whether they are still going out or have begun already to come in.

The island stands off that reach like a chipped tooth, which the wind has scoured to a pale rind of limestone, which no river crosses, which offers a single southern cove deep enough to hold a hull, and there the water is put to work: it is measured by the harbour office, it is photographed by the aircraft that circle from Sicily each dawn, it is written down in the ledgers as so many miles of responsibility.

The rock shelves inland from that cove in terraces of dry stone; men have built on them for four thousand years, sowing barley and burning scrub, because nothing here holds rain for longer than a season.

Above the terraces stands the radar mast, which turns without pause on its lattice; below it lie the long white sheds of the reception centre, whose roofs the gulls have marked and stained.

The apparatus that keeps this coast — and it keeps it thoroughly, courteously, at all hours — is content to describe itself as a service of assistance, so that the cutter which noses out at three in the morning is said to be going to relieve, to succour, to accompany the drifting from danger to a safer shore.

The cove, which the charts still call by its old fishermen's name and which no chart has troubled to rename, whose flagstones the sun bleaches, holds the moored patrol boats in their painted numbers, and behind them the wrecked hulls are stacked in a yard above the tide line, blue and rust and blue again, where the paint peels in long curls and where the timbers, salted through, are left to dry out and to teach the visitor what a crossing costs, since the school groups come down in April and the photographs travel far.

The whole apparatus is careful to instruct, and it instructs by arrangement: the boats are set in rows, the rows are numbered, the numbers are printed on a board at the gate.

The sea beyond obliges the eye to a single motion — it swells, it falls back — and the swell comes in from the southwest and breaks white on the shoal, and the water withdraws again down the shingle before the next one lifts.

Look down from the mast platform on a still morning: the cove shows the hull of the moored cutter twice over, once above the waterline and once beneath it, inverted in the green glass of the shallows, where the stern reverses into the bow and the mast drives downward into the sand and the whole grey shape hangs there, keel uppermost, perfectly legible.

A line runs across that water some twelve miles out, and it is nowhere visible, and it is fixed only by the instruments — by a transponder reading on a screen in an operations room three hundred miles north, which registers the moment of passage — so that a single boat, which is a vessel in distress on the seaward side of the line and which becomes on the landward side a matter for the Republic, changes its name without changing anything of itself, before the crew aboard it have seen so much as a change in the colour of the water, and long after they have ceased to count the hours.

These days the shoreline is receding a little each winter, which the harbour office records without comment.

The wave that comes up the channel, which the pilots on this coast still call the *undulation*, gathers and slackens and gathers again as it runs, and though the mast turns and the ledgers fill and the aircraft go out at dawn over the same ground they covered yesterday, nothing on the water stays where it was put; and the boats keep coming up out of the south, which the island has learned to expect the way it expects weather: they come, they are counted, they are moved on.

The channel that runs south from the last Sicilian headland, hemmed on either hand by nothing but weather, narrows where the shelf lifts under it, and the water, which elsewhere lies open and unmeasured to the horizon, gathers into a running seam of paler blue, so that a vessel entering it seems to be drawn rather than steered; and the island stands at the far end of that seam, a low shard of limestone tilted to the north, whose whole eastern flank drops in a single face to the sea, and whose southern shore breaks into a series of coves so shallow that a hull grounding there ceases to be a hull and becomes, before anyone can name it, a wreck, and then, in the ledger of the port authority, an event.

Lampedusa, which lies nearer to the African shelf than to the continent whose customs it enforces, which the maps assign to one hemisphere and the seabed to another, which the ferries reach in eight hours from Porto Empedocle and the light aircraft in one, is a raft of pale stone thirty metres above the swell; it holds the vessels that arrive here, it holds the men who record their arriving, and it holds, in its single valley, the enclosure where the two are brought together.

Along the north the cliff is unbroken for four kilometres; only at Cala Pisana does the rock relent, and there, where a slipway of poured concrete meets the tide, the launches of the Guardia di Finanza lie moored in a row, bow to stern, grey, riding.

The harbour, which opens eastward beneath the town, is a cut of green water perhaps six hundred metres long; the fishing fleet keeps its western quay, and the patrol boats, whose hulls carry the red diagonal stripe of the state, keep the eastern.

Twelve miles out, a line drawn on no water and visible in no water divides the territorial sea from the contiguous zone, and it is possible to cross it, going north, without any alteration in the swell; the same wave that lifted a boat outside the line and set it down inside is the wave that has changed the boat's legal name, from an object at large to an object to be received.

The southern coast, which the wind seldom troubles enough to whiten, which the guidebooks call the Isola dei Conigli, is a beach of graded shell; and from the ridge above it, where the turtles come ashore in July, where the water shoals through six distinct bands of colour and stands so still at noon that the rock overhead is repeated beneath it, one sees the cliff standing and sees the cliff hanging inverted in the shallows, the two joined at the waterline, and it becomes difficult, unless one looks for the sand between them, to say which face is stone and which is only the sea's account of stone.

The apparatus does not announce itself; it takes the shape of the island, and its instruments sit where the geology puts them.

On the highest ground the radar tower turns; it turns slowly; the mast beside it carries three white dishes, and a fence of galvanised mesh encloses both; the cameras face seaward on their poles, each one panning as the coastguard beneath it drinks his coffee.

The centre stands inland, in the Contrada Imbriacola: a low file of prefabricated blocks, and around them a road, a gate, a roll of wire on the gate, and men at the gate who count what comes through it, who log the count on a printed sheet, who fold the sheet, who pass it up.

Nothing here is hidden; the buildings are visible from the road, and the road is visible from the ridge, from which the whole valley — the blocks, the yard, the wire, the parked coaches — lies open as a plan drawn to scale; and yet the island is described in the official language as a facility of welcome, whose function, as the printed notices posted at the gate declare, is to shelter and to instruct those who arrive without papers, so that the sea, having delivered them, may be relieved of them, and the shore may resume its ordinary business.

At the western end, past the airstrip, the ground falls to a shelf of rock that the swell floods and abandons twice a minute.

That undulation is the island's one continuous fact — it governs the ferry timetable, the fuel deliveries and the hour at which the boats put out — and as one stands there now, in this year of new agreements and new registries, the sea is widening again beyond the shelf, opening out past the twelve-mile line and past the shipping lanes into the enormous unpoliced blue that begins where the arithmetic stops; and the swell that broke on the rock returns to it, a little later, from the south, having gone nowhere at all.

The channel that runs from the Tunisian shelf toward the Sicilian bank, narrowing as it goes between two shoals that carry no name on any chart, widens again below the last of the reefs and the first of the open swells, and continues southward as a corridor of dark water bounded by nothing the eye can hold, which the pilots of the patrol cutters have learned to read by the colour of its surface alone, so that a man who has crossed it once, and who has watched the light go from green to lead, will know, before the instruments confirm it, that he has passed the place where the seabed drops, and where the current, gathering from four directions to make one motion, turns the drift of everything floating eastward.

The island lies athwart that corridor like a stone set down and forgotten, a low grey wedge of limestone tilted toward Africa, whose northern face rises in cliffs of ninety metres and whose southern flank subsides into coves so shallow a hull can ground on sand at the height of the tide; and here the corridor loses its name, for the charts call the water within twelve miles territorial, while the treaties call the same water a zone of contiguous jurisdiction, and the vessels that patrol it call it, simply, the box.

The rock itself is barely eight kilometres end to end; a man can walk its length in a morning, though the walking is hard where the *rutte* of old cart tracks break into scree above the eastern bays.

Nothing grows tall on it but the wind-flattened caper and a scattering of prickly pear that the winter salt burns black each February, and the whole surface reads as a single tilted table, over which the light moves without obstruction from dawn to dusk.

Along the northern rim there are gun emplacements from an older war, filled now with wind-blown plastic and the small bones of birds, and there is a road, unmarked, that runs to serve the radar mast, whose dish turns through its slow arc all night and all day, so that the island appears on screens in Rome and in Warsaw as a fixed white point that never has occasion to move.

Below the mast, in the harbour that gives the island its only deep anchorage, the offshore patrol vessels lie moored stern-to along the quay, painted the pale grey that is meant to disappear against haze, and beside them the smaller craft of the Guardia di Finanza rock at their lines; and on the far side of the basin stands a low building of prefabricated panels, which the signage names a first-reception facility, and which the operational documents describe as a hotspot, where the arrivals are identified and their fingers rolled across a glass plate, and where each person is offered the assistance of the procedure, so that the register may be completed before the transfer is authorized and the ferry, which sails at eleven, is loaded.

The water in that basin is nearly still. You can see the mooring chains lying slack on the bottom in four metres of clear green, and above them, on the underside of the swell, the hull of the cutter hangs inverted, keel uppermost, trembling.

There is a smaller quay beyond it, kept for what the harbourmaster's log calls *unità recuperate*: the boats. They are brought in under tow and stacked, and each is stripped of its outboard, and the wooden ones are lifted by crane onto the concrete and left there, ranked hull to hull, until the yard beyond the fuel tanks is full of them.

The stacking has its own order, for the largest are set at the base and the smallest across the top, and the whole mass settles over a season into something that the eye takes at first for a breakwater, and then for a midden, and then for nothing that has a word.

Seen from the cliff road at evening the island reduces to two elements only: the pale shelf of the rock, and the sea, which is at that hour neither blue nor grey but a burnished undulation running out to a horizon that has no interruption on it whatever. And it is that undulation the visitor remembers — the long swell that crests and slackens and crests, that neither breaks nor stills, and that comes on out of the south all night, gathering as it comes, so that a sound is always present under the sound of the generators and the gulls.

There is a cemetery on the eastern slope, where the graves that carry no name are marked with a number cut into a plate.

But it is on the water, and not on the rock, that the arithmetic is done, for the vessels go out at dusk and the vessels come back at first light, and in the interval between them the sea performs the only labour it knows, which is to enlarge itself in every direction at once; and beyond the twelve-mile line the same swell that lifts the moored cutter is another jurisdiction entirely, over which no one on the island has authority. In these years the line moves outward on the maps, month by month, and the water inside it grows narrower.

The channel that runs south from the last Sicilian headland, between the shelf that shoals under Malta and the deep trench off the African bank, narrows all at once into a corridor of running water, and then, where the seabed lifts again and the swell begins to shorten, it opens and spreads and slackens into a broad tremulous plain, so that a boat leaving Zuwarah at dusk, which the wind and the current together carry north-northeast across it, is thought by the men aboard to be crossing a single named body of water when in fact it passes, hour by hour, out of one authority and into another, the transfers occurring silently, without any change in the colour of the water or in the rhythm at which the hull rises and falls, until the vessel has entered a zone in which every wave it climbs has already been assigned a jurisdiction and a rescue coordination centre.

The island lies low at the corridor's midpoint, a limestone raft tilted eastward, whose southern coast breaks off in sheer white cliffs, whose northern shore descends in terraces of scrub and prickly pear, and whose one deep inlet, the harbour, is the only place along thirty kilometres of rock where a keel may safely touch: everything on Lampedusa turns toward that inlet, as the roads bend toward it, as the fuel drums and the mooring rings gather at its head, as the wind, coming out of the northwest for two hundred days of the year, funnels down into it and lays the water flat.

The rock itself belongs, geologically, to the continent opposite: the island is the tip of the African shelf, drowned and re-emerged, though the maps print it in the colours of Europe and the postal codes begin with nine.

Above the harbour stands a compound of prefabricated units, which the signage calls a centre of first reception and assistance, and beside it, on the slope, a helipad and a fuel store and a mast of white antennae, which turn without pause through the whole of the night.

From the mast the sea is watched in two registers: the visible one, which the eye of a rating on the mole takes in and holds, and the other, invisible, made legible only to the instruments, which read heat rather than light, so that a hull thirty miles out is a smear of warmth on a screen in a room without windows; and the two seas, which no one aboard the smaller boats has any means to distinguish, are watched simultaneously.

The apparatus that has been placed here to save life, and which describes itself in exactly those terms, is a graded thing: the grey cutters at the mole, which sail under one flag and answer to a second; the aircraft out of Sigonella and the drones out of Malta, which fly a lawn-mower pattern and photograph everything and photograph nothing that has not been budgeted; and beneath these, the ledgers, the fingerprint scanners, the identification protocol, which are said to protect the newcomers from exploitation and to instruct them in their rights, so that a man who has walked from Kano is taken gently by the wrist and taught the pressure of ink and glass while a clerk explains the procedure.

Whatever the instruments see, the sea itself keeps no record, and the swell erases in eleven minutes the whole track of a hull.

Consider only the water, then: it thins, it clarifies over the sandy patches, and it darkens and thickens where the shelf drops away, and the light stands down through it in shafts until the shafts are extinguished.

What the surface withholds the surface also renders: the cliff face hangs upside down in the flat morning water below Cala Pulcino, and the sea repeats it inverted, so that the pale rock is doubled by that green mirror, so that the caves become domes, and the loose scree becomes a hanging fringe, and the whole island appears to be sinking.

At dusk the wind drops, and the corridor sets itself in a long low undulation, and the swells come in unhurried, without breaking, in a rhythm that lifts the moored hulls and lets them down again and lifts them; and this undulation, which anyone who has stood a night on the mole learns to feel in the chest before the eye confirms it, which is the same movement that has carried every hull ever driven onto this rock, goes on all night beneath the antennae, seeming to breathe rather than to travel, while the mast turns and the lit compound above the harbour hums.

In this decade the rock is being altered faster than in the previous four thousand years.

There is a stone jetty on the eastern side of the inlet, now half demolished, where the fishing fleet once landed its catch, and since the numbers rose the concrete has been widened and the bollards doubled, so that the boats now come alongside where the nets were once spread, and a new perimeter fence has been run out along the ridge, which the plans designate a screening enclosure; and below it, on the low shelf, the wrecked hulls lie in their painted rows.

The channel that runs south from the Sicilian shelf, hemmed on its eastern flank by a submarine ridge the charts still call the Adventure Bank, narrows where the seafloor climbs and the water changes colour from ink to a scoured green, and delivers at its far end a low limestone island, which lies tilted like a hand held palm-down against the swell, seeming from the air to have been set there by the same current that quarried it, a current which, having no name in the languages of either coast, is measured all the same by instruments moored offshore, since the agencies that fund them require, in order to plan, that the drift be known before the season turns, so that the boats may be counted and the counting filed.

The island is nine kilometres of rock that carries no river, that holds its rainwater in cisterns cut by hands nobody remembers, that offers the arriving eye a single harbour to enter and a single road to climb; the cliffs stand white above the water, the prickly pear grows where the goats have not yet reached it, and the wind out of Africa lays a fine ochre dust on every windward sill.

Southward the water dilates into an immense unbroken plain that seems to have no shore at all; there is nothing between here and the Gulf of Sirte but weather, and the horizon holds itself flat and shining until the light goes out of it.

North of the island the channel contracts between two shelves whose edges the fishermen know by the drag on their nets; the fetch shortens there, and the swell that came in long from the open sea steepens into short seas that break on nothing.

The harbour of the town narrows to a throat of pale rock that the ferries and the patrol craft share, and the whole body of the sea seems to gather itself in order to press through it when the northwesterlies run; then it widens again inside, into a green basin whose floor you can read from the quay wall, sand and weed and the shadow of a hull.

Above the basin stands the pier where the grey cutters lie, hulls that seem to have been designed to be seen from a distance, hulls whose flanks carry the blue lettering of the coastal service, and the water beneath them holds each vessel twice: once as a shape a man sees plainly, and once as a longer, wavering shape the swell turns upside down, the mirror lengthening it, the mirror breaking it whenever a wake crosses, so that the reflection seems to reach for the seabed while the true hull sits high and the paintwork dries.

The apparatus is disposed across this rock as a geology is disposed: the radar mast to command the northern arc, and the thermal lens turning all night on its pedestal above the cemetery.

A vessel crossing north is at one moment a matter for one authority and at the next for another; nothing in the water marks the change; the swell does not alter, the colour does not alter, and only the plotted position on a screen ashore declares that the boat has ceased to be a foreign object and has begun to be an obligation, since the line it crossed exists in a treaty and nowhere else.

The instruments hold their own weather: the mast turns and the lens sweeps, and the sea beneath them keeps the arrangement it has always kept, rising where the shelf rises and falling away where the shelf falls, so that a swell built off the Gulf runs unbroken for four hundred miles and arrives here as a slow, legible undulation, an undulation that lifts the moored boats and sets them down.

The island is the seaward salient of a system: the ridge under the water carries the current, and the current carries whatever floats on it toward this one landfall, a landfall that shelters the arriving and registers them, that offers water and a blanket and a number; and around this the buildings have arranged themselves in the manner of scree, low blocks behind a fence which stands on the site of an older airfield, where in these years the fence is being extended a metre at a time, seeming to grow the way the rock grows, that is, by the removal of everything softer.

Nothing on the island rises high enough to see over the horizon that surrounds it on every side.

The sea here goes out and comes back within a single hour and within a single decade, a rhythm that the harbourmaster's log has recorded since the log began, and because the water swells and subsides, and because the drift that brings the boats is the same drift that brought the tuna the nets once waited for, the island lives by what the current delivers and by what it takes away, a delivery no schedule governs; the mast turns, the cutter sails, the swell rises and subsides.

The channel that narrows between the Pelagie shelf and the African margin, running south by a hand's breadth off the last Sicilian stone, comes down in two long arms of rock to the place where the sea, gathering its whole northward weight, is pressed into a strait and lets go of it again, and the shoals there, which the fishermen still name for the men lost above them, break the current into braids and counter-braids that seem, when the wind stands from the southeast and the swell begins to build under a sky the colour of dry salt, to run uphill toward the island, so that a boat setting out from Zuwarah at dusk, drifting rather than steering, arrives by morning at a coastline it never chose and finds the shore already counted, mapped, and waiting.

The island itself, which lies low and pale as a cuttlebone on the water, whose highest ground would not shade a mast, whose bays open like fingers to receive whatever the current has carried, seems built to be arrived at and never to be left; the airstrip lengthens toward the cliff, the concrete jetty runs out past the last house, the white boats of the guard lie moored with their engines cooling while the harbour breathes, while the buoys nod in their chains, while the light on the mole turns and turns above the sleeping berths.

South of the fishing quay a wire fence descends the slope to the beach, and it holds nothing back, since the sea itself has already been enlisted, tightening and slackening around the rock as reliably as any patrol.

There is a hangar above the runway whose doors stand open on rows of orange hulls, stacked and stripped and numbered, and the plaque beside it thanks the ships that assisted them, which took them from the water and delivered them to the yard.

The waters here have long been divided by lines that no eye finds and no keel disturbs, and a vessel crossing them is said to pass from search into interception, though nothing changes in the swell beneath it, nothing in the wind; the change is written in a logbook, which a duty officer signs to make it true.

The lamp on the coastguard tower, which is set high enough to be seen from the shipping lane, which sweeps the offing every eleven seconds, throws a white bar across the harbour, and the water beneath it takes the beam and returns it, doubled and reversed, so that a watcher on the jetty sees the tower standing upright on the rock and sees it also hanging inverted in the black basin, its light travelling downward into a sky the water keeps, and the two towers move together whenever a wake crosses and the reflected one shivers into rings.

The current in the strait does not rest; it goes on gathering along the shelf, and it thins again in the lee of the headland.

The wind rises in the afternoon to comb the shallows white, and then it drops, and the surface flattens and lies down, and the sound comes back over the rock when the gulls have gone.

The whole coast keeps this rhythm: the tide fills the inlets and empties them, while the boats put out and return, and the launches go down the channel, and the radar arm turns in its cage above the port.

By the reckoning of this present decade the shoreline is changing, for the beaches thin each winter, and the dunes retreat behind their fences, which the storms of February open and the summer closes; and the low ground behind the reception centre, which was once a field of caper and thorn, whose stones the farmers cleared, is now a graded apron of gravel where the buses stand in line to be filled at first light before the ferry is called.

Everything on the island is arranged around an arrival that nobody on the island has arranged.

The rock at the southern point, which drops sheer into water so clear that the bottom seems within reach, holds the eye longest, because the sea there is at its widest and because the horizon, which shows nothing at all, gives back no measure of the distance; and the fence gate stands open above it, which the wind swings on its hinge, and the boats come in from the south, and the light turns, and the sea closes over the place it opened.

The channel that runs south from the last Sicilian headland, narrowing where the shelf drops and the water darkens, is held on either flank by two unequal masses of stone, the African plate and the European, which have been grinding toward one another since before there were names for either, and it opens at its middle into a shallow basin where a single low island lies, so pale in its limestone that pilots take it for a cloud shadow, an island that seems less to rise from the sea than to be forgotten by it, since the swell that leaves the Gulf of Gabès arrives here with its force already spent, having crossed sixty leagues of open water to lose, in that crossing, the weight it gathered when it first left the sand and turned north.

Lampedusa is the name the charts give it, a chip of dolomite tilted so that its northern face stands in cliffs above the water, its southern face slopes gently into coves and shingle, its whole length measured at nine kilometres by the surveyors sent to establish what the state possessed; and the sea makes the island what it is, for it is the sea that scours the tables of rock bare, it is the sea that lays the fine warm sand in the southern bays, it is the sea that carries, out of the dark beyond the shipping lanes, whatever the season sends.

Nothing on the island is high enough to be called a hill; and yet the ground rises steadily from the harbour, so that a man walking inland finds the horizon opening behind him at every step, blue and unbroken and entirely without incident.

The harbour itself is a long crooked inlet, which the water enters slowly and leaves slowly, a natural basin scoured by nothing; and at its head stands the mole, along which the grey hulls tie up in the evening with their engines still turning.

From the mole the eye follows a line of quays and slipways, which begin at the fuel pontoon and end at the last bollard, seeming to gather the whole settlement toward the water as if the island had been built facing outward; and beyond them lies the boatyard, where the confiscated hulls are stacked to dry in the sun.

The vessels that the patrol brings in, drawn up on the concrete to be counted and photographed, are of a wood that no local carpenter uses, painted in blues and greens that hold their colour badly; and each is registered in a ledger that lists its length, its beam, and the number of persons the rescuers assisted from it, figures which are entered in ink and copied to Rome, and figures which are read aloud at intervals in rooms far to the north, to be set against other figures whenever the season turns and the arrivals rise and the ledger fills again.

The apparatus, to give it the name it gives itself, keeps the water under observation, and the observation is continuous.

The radar mast, turning to sweep the channel, sees nothing that the sea does not carry; the drone above it sees further, and the aerostat further still, and what all three see is transmitted to the operations room, where the coast is drawn in green light as the machine understands it.

The screen shows the coastline twice: the true shore glows along the lower margin, and the same shore appears again inverted in the black glass above the console, so that the officer on watch reads the island and reads its reflection, and cannot always say which line is stone and which is only light and which is the low cloud coming in.

Twelve miles out, an unmarked line crosses the water: on one side of it a boat in distress is a matter for the coastguard, and on the other it is a matter for no one, or for whichever authority accepts the call, which is a distinction the sea itself does not register, since nothing on the surface changes. Only the plotter changes, printing a new set of coordinates, which convert the same hull, at the same speed, on the same swell, into a different object under a different law, without the crew aboard perceiving it, and without the water darkening by a shade.

Everything here is arranged for the water to be seen, and nothing for the seeing to be seen.

Along the southern shore the swell returns each autumn, running up the coves as it has always run, and the reef offshore takes the weight of it, so that the beach receives only the last smooth undulation, the long lucid heaving that carries in what it carries; and in these years the sand is rising, which the harbourmaster attributes to the dredging; the island, meanwhile, goes on lying pale in its shallow basin, low, bare, and lit from every side.

The channel that runs south from the last shoal of Sicily, narrowing where two continental shelves lean toward one another and the water darkens over the trench between them, widens again below the parallel into a shallow basin the fishermen still call the Mattress, and here it lays down, on a floor of sand and broken coral, the long spine of rock that surfaces at last as Lampedusa, so that a vessel coming up from the south, whose crew have watched three nights of open swell, sees the island lift as a low grey line and then, as the light hardens, begins to make out, before the harbour opens, before the first breakwater declares itself, the quarry cuts and the aerial masts and the white cubes of the reception centre stacked in the valley behind the town.

The island itself, which is nine kilometres of limestone tilted like a dropped tray, whose northern edge stands two hundred feet above the water in one unbroken cliff, whose southern edge slopes down through terraces of prickly pear and dry wall to be met by the sea in a series of small coves, keeps its whole weather on one side: the north face takes the maestrale and holds it, the south face lies in shelter through nine months of the year, and the wind that crosses the ridge arrives on the far slope thinned to a warm and constant breathing.

Along that sheltered flank the coves open one after another, each a bite of white shingle between two headlands — Cala Croce, Cala Galera, Cala Pisana — where the water shelves so gradually that a hull can ground a hundred metres out and the people aboard walk in.

The harbour is a single crooked inlet, whose mouth faces east and takes the morning directly; and along its inner arm lie the boats that have been brought in and are kept, a yard of hulls in blue and rust and open ribs, which the salt is eating at its own pace.

Above the yard the coastguard station holds the height, whose windows face the entrance and whose masts carry the radar that turns all night; and the beam sweeps out to trace the arc of the approaches, contracting as it passes over the near water and dilating over the far, while the screens below register each return as a small green blossom that opens, fades, and is written to a log.

The sea that lies between this rock and the Libyan shore, which needs a day and a half to cross in calm and is never calm for a day and a half together, which every chart divides into zones of responsibility by lines no eye can find, is one water and one weight; and it is the instruments that decide which name it wears, the transponder that reports a position, the log that records an hour, so that a hull afloat in one minute is a matter for Tripoli and in the next a matter for Rome, the boundary being nothing in itself, having no colour and no smell and no change of swell, and the crossing of it being knowable only because a machine in a room ashore has stamped the moment and filed it and gone on.

The patrol boats go out at dusk to stand off the southern approaches, and the fishing fleet goes out with them, and the two sets of lights ride the same slow water at the same slow interval.

From the cliff at Albero Sole one can see the whole of the western sea at once; the horizon is a hard rule; the low cloud stands above it and the same cloud stands inverted beneath it, doubled in the polished calm; and the eye takes the water plainly while the water takes the sky back to itself reversed, so that the island appears to float in a substance made of its own weather.

In summer the surface tightens to a skin, and it holds so still that a swimmer's wake will travel a hundred metres before it dies, and the cliffs give back their heat all night, and the rock cools, and the cisterns sweat, and nothing on the whole island moves except the radar.

Then in October the water begins to breathe again, and the swell comes long and grey from the northwest, and the coves fill with a surf that scours out the summer's rubbish, which the winter storms carry off and bury and now and then return; and it is the undulation of that season, running under the hulls that lie moored in the harbour, that lifts them and sets them down and lifts them again through the night, that will not let them rest, so that anyone standing on the mole at three in the morning learns, before he has learned anything else about this place, before he has heard a single word spoken in the reception centre, what it is that the sea does to what floats on it.

The undulation is the island's one continuous fact, which the rock resists and the boats confess.

In these years, while I write, the town is changing around that fact: the fishing quays that once held forty boats now hold twelve, and the money moves through the island in the form of contracts for security and rescue and provision, so that the new work is the care of arrivals, and the old work goes on beside it in a diminished way; the centre in the valley calls its rooms halls of hospitality and its high fence a measure for the protection of guests, and the ferry manifest carries them off at dawn to the mainland; and the sea, dilating again under the first weather of autumn, brings the next boats up the same channel.
